Pulmonology · published research

Lung injury

In an LPS rat model, 660-nm red laser reduced ventilatory impairment, inflammatory markers, and tissue injury. An 808-nm laser changed selected cytokines with partial tissue improvement but no lung-mechanics benefit, while 430-nm LED affected only selected cytokines.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In an LPS rat model, 660-nm red laser reduced ventilatory impairment, inflammatory markers, and tissue injury. An 808-nm laser changed selected cytokines with partial tissue improvement but no lung-mechanics benefit, while 430-nm LED affected only selected cytokines.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Respiratory system > Lung injury category contains 16 rodent publications, 11 using rats and five using mice. Four publications also include cell experiments; these are overlapping methods within the animal papers, not four additional independent titles. No human clinical study is listed.

Human and clinical evidence

No direct human PBM treatment study for acute or other lung injury was identified in the assigned category.

Animal evidence

Models include lipopolysaccharide injury, sepsis, ventilator-induced injury, and systemic injury. A 2026 study induced lung injury with LPS in 288 male Wistar rats and compared several light spectra. The 660-nm red laser was the only tested exposure that reduced all measured ventilatory-mechanics parameters, myeloperoxidase activity, inflammatory cytokines, and histological injury. The 808-nm infrared laser reduced TNF-alpha and IL-6 with partial histological improvement but did not improve lung mechanics; 430-nm blue LED affected selected cytokines without mechanical or histological benefit (Figueiredo et al. 2026). Other animal reports examine sepsis-related inflammation and macrophage responses (Pan et al. 2024 Zhang et al. 2026).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Four publications include cultured cells or cell-level assays alongside an animal model. These experiments can help explain mechanisms but are not standalone human evidence.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Reported spectra include 430-nm blue LED, 660-nm red laser, and 808-nm near-infrared laser. Wavelength is the light's color band and affects how far it can travel through tissue. The differing results within one animal model show why results from one wavelength or endpoint should not be transferred to another.

Interpretation

Several rodent studies report changes in inflammatory or tissue outcomes, but effects differ by spectrum and measure. No patient-level benefit has been demonstrated. Future work should reproduce lung-function outcomes and report dose, timing, and adverse effects clearly.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for selected inflammatory and ventilatory outcomes in induced rodent injury models No direct human treatment evidence identified
Publications and records16 titles (exact Respiratory system > Lung injury)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Sixteen rodent publications examine different causes and phases of lung injury, and four include cell experiments. A recent multi-arm study found effects that differed by light color and outcome. Human studies are absent. Independent replication should clarify which settings change lung function rather than biomarkers alone.
